http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/six-c.text: Days after Colombia's newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in, and who had vowed a battle against crime as a major part of his campaign, the leader announced the killings of six members of armed groups by Colombian forces on Sunday.The far-right leader promised a fight against criminal groups that were profiting from drug trafficking as the country experiences its worst wave of violence in the past decade.In a statement, the far-right leader said the operation was intended to send a clear and forceful message to all criminals in Colombia. "There is nowhere for them to hide when the State is determined to act. I have given specific instructions to law enforcement agencies to carry out all necessary operations that were held back by the previous administration (of Gustavo Petro)," said De la Espriella.Sunday's military operations marked the new administration's first actions against illegal groups, which campaigned on a pledge to confront "narcoterrorism without truce".In a show of force, President Abelardo de la Espriella's swearing-in ceremony was held in the southwestern city of Cali, which is known for its high violence and crime rates.De la Espriella wants to build mega-prisons similar to the one in El Salvador and increase airstrikes against guerrillas and narco traffickers.The six killed by Colombian forces on Sunday include four members of a splinter faction of the former FARC guerrilla group, as well as two members of the Gulf Clan, Colombia's main drug cartel, in Antioquia department in the northwest.Meanwhile, on Saturday, De la Espriella's first day in office was marred by two separate bombings, leaving at least one police officer dead and wounding several people. FARC guerrilla members used explosives to destroy a highway tollbooth near Cali, with two security guards suffering minor injuries, according to Colombia's army.

Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen Claire escaped an abusive partner in the US and was given nine days’ notice to appear in court. Photograph: AlexLinch/Getty Images/iStockphoto Domestic violence Hope for UK mothers accused of child abduction after fleeing domestic violence Women escaping abusive partners abroad could get new protections from legal analysis of Hague convention Amelia Hill Tue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 00.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google British mothers who bring their children with them when returning to the UK after fleeing from domestic abuse abroad – which can lead to them being accused of abduction – could be given greater legal protection and support. The government has agreed to examine how domestic abuse features in international child abduction cases, with a view to giving survivors of domestic abuse more help fighting partners’ demands that they return children to their home countries. The changes would come too late for Claire, who lived in the US with an abusive partner and their two small children for more than a decade. But they could help mothers like her. “We were all terrified of him. I was in near-constant fear for my life,” she said. “Eventually, I escaped and got us all on a plane back home to the UK.” She lived in hiding for three months, but eventually had to apply for benefits. “Within a day, the police were at our door with summons under the Hague convention to appear in court just nine days later,” she said. Approximately 500 Hague-convention applications for the return of a child are filed each year in England and Wales. Between 10% and 20% of children affected end up being separated from their primary carer owing to a formal court-ordered return. Claire was fortunate: she used all of her savings to instruct a barrister, and her children were able to stay in the UK. “I barely stood any chance even with legal representation – all my evidence of the domestic abuse was ignored,” she said. “It was only because my barrister persuaded the judge to let my oldest child, who was a few weeks short of the 14 years when courts will listen to their views, give evidence that I won the case.” The new analysis, to be carried out by the Ministry of Justice’s private international family law team, will look at all cases held in the high court in London between 2024 and 2025 under the 1980 Hague convention. The convention requires signatory countries to return children who have been unilaterally removed abroad within six weeks so that courts in their home countries can decide on future arrangements. Campaigners hope the analysis, the first of its kind, will disprove the four-decade-old assumptions, baked into the convention, that all child abduction is harmful and that children must be returned immediately for overseas courts to decide their futures. Ruth Dineen, international coordinator of the Filia Hague Mothers campaign , said the convention had been introduced in 1980 to protect children from the harmful effects of their wrongful removal from their home country. “But the circumstances surrounding international child abduction have changed substantially since then,” she said. “There are far more relationships between parents of different nationalities, so it’s much more common for families to live abroad. We also have a far greater understanding of the impact of domestic abuse and coercive control.” Roz Osborne, head of the charity Globalarrk , said she hoped the government analysis would help level the playing field for victims of domestic abuse. “At the moment, victims do not have access to equal legal support, due to legal aid inequalities, which causes delay or – worse – no legal representation at all for the victim survivor,” she said. “Where respondents do not meet the means and merits test and pay, they can lose substantial funds, even when winning their case, putting them in debt. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “Victims have no access to emotional support in the high court, via a domestic abuse support worker,” she added. Summary hearings do not allow sufficient understanding of the risks victims face, often underestimating the risks. Children’s safety is inseparable from their primary carer’s safety, most often the mother, and this is not recognised.” In addition, she said, children were not acknowledged as victims in their own right, as they are under domestic abuse legislation in the UK. Dr Adrienne Barnett, the director of Right to Equality, said there was a “dearth of basic data” around these cases. “On top of not knowing how often domestic violence is alleged and found, we don’t even know what percentage of returning parents are mothers,” she said. “We don’t know how many cases end in children being returned without their parent, whether the children say they don’t want to be sent home or what protective measures are put in place when they are.” Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP and long-term campaigner on the shortcomings of the Hague convention, said the analysis was long overdue. “A parent – often but not always the mother – who escapes to this country to protect themselves and their children from violence should not find themselves faced with a legal mechanism that treats them as a wrongdoer,” she said. “Yet that is precisely the situation too many find themselves in.” A Home Office spokesperson said there was no timeline for the new research but that it was “intended to provide robust evidence to inform possible future government policy on the effective operation of the convention in England and Wales in these complex and sensitive cases”. Alison Shalaby, the chief executive of Reunite, said it remained vital that children were returned immediately to their parents when abducted. “The Hague convention provides a clear, unbiased court process that the left-behind parent can follow,” she said. “It provides plenty of defences and opportunities for parents under the convention in England and Wales, where legal aid is available where there is domestic abuse.” In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid . In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org . https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/two.text: The Budapest Times Two wheels, new deal: scooter rules finally get a facelift Motorized scooters will become a separate vehicle category in the Hungarian Highway Code (KRESZ), their use will be prohibited under the influence of alcohol, and carrying a second person on them will also be banned — Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on his Facebook page on Wednesday late afternoon, according to the government's proposal. In his video, the Prime Minister stated that following extensive professional consultations and after hearing the opinions of several hundred thousand people, the government has decided to amend and tighten the Highway Code in order to meaningfully reduce the number of scooter-related accidents. The regulation will be put to public debate once more before it is officially promulgated. According to the government’s proposal, the motorized scooter will become a separate vehicle category in the Highway Code, with specific rules applying to it — including a prohibition on use while under the influence of alcohol and a ban on carrying a second person. High-powered electric scooters will be prohibited from using the pavement in all cases, while low-powered electric scooters will only be permitted to do so when no other alternative option is available, such as a cycle path. Under the government’s proposal, electric scooters will henceforth be classified into two vehicle categories based on their power output. Those capable of reaching a maximum speed of 25 kilometres per hour will be considered low-powered scooters; the minimum age for their use will be 14, and the wearing of a helmet will be compulsory up to the age of 18. Every device with a maximum speed exceeding 25 kilometres per hour will fall into the high-powered motorised scooter category; these will be permitted for use by those aged 16 and over. Riding them will be subject to obtaining at least a licence for mopeds and scooters, and the use of a crash helmet will also be mandatory. For high-powered motorised scooters, the maximum speed will be 40 kilometres per hour. For rental electric scooters, the top speed will be capped at 20 kilometres per hour, the Prime Minister explained. Péter Magyar also spoke about the fact that electric scooters have spread explosively in Hungary in recent years, becoming one of the most common modes of transport within just a few years, with tens of thousands of people using them daily, while the existing regulations do not even recognise this vehicle category. He added that these devices are predominantly used by young people. He added that the number of accidents related to the use of electric scooters has risen dramatically in recent years. “Until now, governments have swept this problem under the rug — they were not even willing to acknowledge its existence. While they talked endlessly about protecting our children, they failed to notice the very danger that every parent, every doctor, and every road safety expert outside their circle could see,” he remarked. He added that the Tisza government had begun addressing the problem practically on its first day in office. In his words, electric scooters make transportation more efficient and sustainable, “which is why it was a difficult question to determine where to draw the lines and what rules to introduce.” He recalled that in the summer they had launched a public consultation on road safety, one of the most important topics of which was the regulation of electric scooters, and that in less than two months more than three hundred thousand people had shared their views. A representative opinion poll was also conducted on the subject, consultations were held with transport experts, and European regulations were reviewed as well. He indicated that participants in the public consultation and the representative survey, as well as the experts, all agreed that the regulation of electric scooters needed to happen as soon as possible.
